Lecture 24

Fourier operational rules and distributional transforms

We prove the operational rules of the Fourier transform for integrable functions and check them on a Gaussian wave packet. We prove that exponential decay of a function makes its transform analytic in a strip. We define the transform of a tempered distribution by duality and compute the transforms of deltas, constants, sinusoids and the step, and we write the step as a regularized integral over wave numbers.

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

  • Compute a transform with the shift, modulation, scaling, derivative and multiplication rules, and track every phase, scale factor and sign of the convention.
  • State the hypotheses of each rule, and recognize when a jump of the function invalidates the ordinary derivative rule.
  • Decide from the exponential decay of a function on which strip of the complex plane its transform is analytic.
  • Transform deltas, constants, sinusoids and the step as tempered distributions, by test-function pairing and by regularization, and say which identities hold only in the sense of tempered distributions.

Lecture 23 defined the Fourier transform of an integrable function, computed the transforms of a rectangular pulse, a Gaussian and decaying exponentials, and proved two inversion theorems. In this lecture we derive rules that produce new transforms from known ones. They describe the effect of a shift, a modulation, a change of scale, a derivative and a multiplication by xxx. We then show that a function with exponential decay has a transform that is analytic in a strip of the complex kkk-plane. Finally, we extend the transform to the tempered distributions of Lecture 22. The extension assigns transforms to the delta, to constants and sinusoids, and to the step, none of which is integrable. The lecture reads in three stages: the ordinary rules and the strip (Sections 24.1–24.2), duality (Section 24.3), and the distributional pairs with the card (Sections 24.4–24.5).

24.1 Rules for integrable functions

A shift multiplies the transform by a phase, a modulation moves it along the kkk-axis, and a compression of fff (∣c∣>1\abs c>1∣c∣>1) stretches f^\widehat ff​ by the factor ∣c∣\abs c∣c∣, the reciprocal relation of widths seen in Lecture 23.

The next two rules connect the smoothness of fff with the decay of f^\widehat ff​, and conversely. Piecewise C1C^1C1 functions are those of Lecture 23.

24.2 Analyticity in a strip

Lecture 18 showed that the transform of a Gaussian extends to an entire function of kkk, because of the fast decay of the Gaussian. Exponential decay of fff already gives analyticity of f^\widehat ff​ in a strip. For a>0a>0a>0 let Ua={k∈C:∣Im⁡k∣<a}U_a=\{k\in\C:\abs{\Im k}<a\}Ua​={k∈C:∣Imk∣<a} be the open strip of width 2a2a2a about the real axis.

The proof below applies Lecture 18’s lemma on analytic parameter integrals to the entire functions k↦e−ikxf(x)k\mapsto\ee^{-\iu kx}f(x)k↦e−ikxf(x).

Let fff be piecewise continuous on every bounded interval, let a>0a>0a>0, and let ∫Rea∣x∣∣f(x)∣ ⁣dx<∞.\int_{\R}\ee^{a\abs x}\abs{f(x)}\dd x<\infty .∫R​ea∣x∣∣f(x)∣dx<∞.(24.7) Then for every k∈Uak\in U_ak∈Ua​ the integral f^(k)=12π∫Re−ikxf(x) ⁣dx\widehat f(k)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{\R}\ee^{-\iu kx}f(x)\dd xf​(k)=2π​1​∫R​e−ikxf(x)dx converges absolutely. Definition 24.11 (Fourier transform of a tempered distribution). Let TTT be a tempered distribution on R\RR. Its Fourier transform T^=F ⁣[T]\widehat T=\FT TT=F[T] and its inverse Fourier transform F−1 ⁣[T]\IFT TF−1[T] are the linear maps on S(R)\Schwartz(\R)S(R) given by ⟨T^,ψ⟩=⟨T,ψ^⟩,⟨F−1 ⁣[T],ψ⟩=⟨T,F−1 ⁣[ψ]⟩(ψ∈S(R)).\distpair{\widehat T}{\psi}=\distpair{T}{\widehat\psi},\qquad \distpair{\IFT T}{\psi}=\distpair{T}{\IFT\psi}\qquad(\psi\in\Schwartz(\R)).⟨T,ψ⟩=⟨T,ψ​⟩,⟨F−1[T],ψ⟩=⟨T,F−1[ψ]⟩(ψ∈S(R)).

  • Temperedness: the transforms T^\widehat TT and F−1 ⁣[T]\IFT TF−1[T] are tempered distributions.

The continuity property licenses regularization: approximate a tempered distribution by integrable functions, transform them as functions, and take the limit.

The transform is defined on S(R)\Schwartz(\R)S(R) rather than on the smaller class D(R)\testspace(\R)D(R) for the following reason. For ψ∈D(R)\psi\in\testspace(\R)ψ∈D(R) condition (24.7) holds for every a>0a>0a>0, so ψ^\widehat\psiψ​ extends to an entire function by Theorem 24.7. So ψ^∉D(R)\widehat\psi\notin\testspace(\R)ψ​∈/D(R) for every nonzero ψ∈D(R)\psi\in\testspace(\R)ψ∈D(R), and a distribution that acts only on D(R)\testspace(\R)D(R) cannot be paired with ψ^\widehat\psiψ​. The function ex\ee^xex of Lecture 22 defines such a distribution, which is not tempered, and it has no Fourier transform in the sense of Definition 24.11.

The operational rules extend to tempered distributions. We use Lecture 22’s definitions of translation, scaling and multiplication, with tests ψ∈S(R)\psi\in\Schwartz(\R)ψ∈S(R), for multiplication by xxx and by eiαx\ee^{\iu\alpha x}eiαx only: multiplication by an arbitrary smooth function does not preserve S(R)\Schwartz(\R)S(R) (ex2e−x2=1\ee^{x^2}\ee^{-x^2}=1ex2e−x2=1). The functions ψ(⋅+x0)\psi(\cdot+x_0)ψ(⋅+x0​), ψ(⋅/c)\psi(\cdot/c)ψ(⋅/c), xψx\psixψ and eiαxψ\ee^{\iu\alpha x}\psieiαxψ lie again in S(R)\Schwartz(\R)S(R), with seminorms bounded by finite combinations of seminorms of ψ\psiψ, so these operations produce tempered distributions from tempered distributions.

24.4 Distributional transforms

We now compute the transforms of the basic tempered distributions of Lecture 22. None of them is an integrable function, so none has a transform in the sense of Lecture 23.

Proposition 24.18 (A regularized integral for the step). Let ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0. The limit against every ψ∈S(R)\psi\in\Schwartz(\R)ψ∈S(R) was shown in the proof of Proposition 24.17, and D(R)⊂S(R)\testspace(\R)\subset\Schwartz(\R)D(R)⊂S(R). ■

So the formula Θ(x)=lim⁡ε→0+(2πi)−1∫eikx ⁣dk/(k−iε)\Heaviside(x)=\lim_{\varepsilon\to0^+}(2\pi\iu)^{-1}\int\ee^{\iu kx}\dd k/(k-\iu\varepsilon)Θ(x)=limε→0+​(2πi)−1∫eikxdk/(k−iε) holds for every x≠0x\ne0x=0 and in the sense of distributions. At x=0x=0x=0 it holds only with the principal value, which gives the symmetric value Θ(0)=12\Heaviside(0)=\tfrac12Θ(0)=21​. Lecture 23’s inversion with symmetric cutoffs, applied to e−εxΘ(x)\ee^{-\varepsilon x}\Heaviside(x)e−εxΘ(x), gives the same values as limits over [−R,R][-R,R][−R,R], with the half-sum 12\tfrac1221​ at x=0x=0x=0.

Summary

The shift, modulation, scaling and conjugation rules hold for every integrable function. The derivative rule needs a continuous function with an integrable derivative; a jump adds a term that only the distributional derivative records. Exponential decay makes the transform analytic in a strip. The multiplication formula moves the transform onto tests in S(R)\Schwartz(\R)S(R); this defines the transform of every tempered distribution, such as deltas, constants, sinusoids and the step.

  • Rules: the first table of Section 24.5, each with its hypotheses; F ⁣[f′]=ikf^\FT{f'}=\iu k\widehat fF[f′]=ikf​ needs a continuous fff.

  • Strip: if ∫ea∣x∣∣f∣ ⁣dx<∞\int\ee^{a\abs x}\abs{f}\dd x<\infty∫ea∣x∣∣f∣dx<∞ with a>0a>0a>0, then f^\widehat ff​ is analytic on ∣Im⁡k∣<a\abs{\Im k}<a∣Imk∣<a; for e−a∣x∣\ee^{-a\abs x}e−a∣x∣ the strip ∣Im⁡k∣<a\abs{\Im k}<a∣Imk∣<a cannot be widened.

  • Tempered transforms: ⟨T^,ψ⟩=⟨T,ψ^⟩\distpair{\widehat T}{\psi}=\distpair{T}{\widehat\psi}⟨T,ψ⟩=⟨T,ψ​⟩ for ψ∈S(R)\psi\in\Schwartz(\R)ψ∈S(R); the pairs of the second table; ex\ee^xex is not tempered and has no transform.

  • Step: in the sense of tempered distributions, 1/(k−iε)→pv⁡(1/k)+iπδ1/(k-\iu\varepsilon)\to\pv(1/k)+\iu\pi\dirac1/(k−iε)→pv(1/k)+iπδ; for x≠0x\ne0x=0, (2πi)−1∫eikx ⁣dk/(k−iε)=e−εxΘ(x)(2\pi\iu)^{-1}\int\ee^{\iu kx}\dd k/(k-\iu\varepsilon)=\ee^{-\varepsilon x}\Heaviside(x)(2πi)−1∫eikxdk/(k−iε)=e−εxΘ(x); at x=0x=0x=0 the principal value is 12\tfrac1221​.

The transform of a product is not the product of the transforms; Lecture 25 shows that the transform of a convolution is.
